Which is “LEAFIER”. Oak, eh? Okay, let’s drill down a bit.

If fir needles are not leaves, then of course oak wins and word puzzle trickery reigns absolutely. But fir needles are leaves. 

So what do our eyes tell us? When we look at a tree and quesstimate which is “leafier”, we tend to see something roughly based on “projected leaf area”. And again, of course oak leaves have more area than fir leaves - not only each leaf, but (probably, it seems, and also according to the data) total for trees of about the same size (whatever that means).

However, while leaf area is functionally very important for how efficiently a tree intercepts light and exchanges CO2 and O2 with the air, I think the real measure of which tree is “LEAFIER” (has more investment in its leaves, relative to its total size) is a measure called Leaf Mass Index: (total leaf mass)/(total tree* mass). And here, conifers (almost) always win out over deciduous species. Oak leaves are light weights, while needles are typically structurally rigid and thus denser and thicker and heavier, for an equal amount of total wood mass supporting them and produced by them.

It’s a complex, if not blurry, area of study, but I say conifers are leafier than deciduous trees (which are woodier).

And this time of year, I could take a crystal clear photo showing a very un-leafy oak tree next to “a fir, green”. The truth is out there.


*practically speaking, only above-ground tree mass is usually measured or estimated.

Someone posted in an earlier comment a disdain for NdgT for his support of the declassification of Pluto. This sent me down a rabbit hole as to the definition of a planet and why this is still a contentious issue. The short version is, if Earth and Pluto swapped positions, Pluto would be classified as a planet, but Earth would not (it becomes a dwarf planet). Those against the declassification of Pluto argue that location should not define a planet, using this example. Further adding to the controversy is that the 2006 vote took place on the last day of the IAU conference, after 95% of the delegates had left, leaving only 5% to determine Pluto's fate. I say Make Pluto a Planet Again!

The fir probably wins out, too, if you consider LEAF area. 

Also: I have no problem at all with Pluto being demoted. It is mind-boggling to me that anyone would hate NdGT for agreeing with the current definition. Weird.

@Steve L I suspect it’s a larger holiday in Canada than in the US. We wear the poppy and hold large public ceremonies that a lot of people attend. We have a nationally televised ceremony on TV, and schoolchildren have assemblies for moments of silence.
With respect to your second post. We do have parades here and we do wear poppies. There are various wreath laying ceremonies and remarks from leaders.

There are many public ceremonies here, including a big parade in Manhattan, but schoolchildren don't have assemblies for the moment of silence because most of them are off for the day.

I think people think NdGT and others have a specific vendetta against Pluto which is not the case. 

Before the IAU 2006 summit there wasnt a clear, scientifically agreed definition of what a planet. ‘Planets’ were being discovered much more regularly than before so there became a need to define what a planet was specifically, otherwise any large spherical space object could be called a planet by its discoverer and then the term planet would no longer be a useful term to describe anything. 

It was decided that planets must meet 3 conditions to be called a planet, one of those conditions is that the object has to gravitational dominance around its orbit or has ‘cleared its neighbourhood’ of similar sized objects and debris. 

Pluto has not ‘cleared its neighbourhood’ (Neptune crosses its orbit) so it can’t be called a planet. If it switched places with Earth it likely would still not have a clear orbit, it’s not just about it position around the Sun.
